title: Continuous agile development and operations
blurb: Apply DevOps, continuous delivery and production monitoring so a product stays deployable and keeps improving with little friction.
question: Pinewick Home and Garden's e-commerce team deploys small changes several times a week, but the IT operations manager wants every change held for a weekly change board. Which approach BEST reflects continuous agile development and operations?

teach.body: Continuous agile development and operations is a set of practices for rapid, automated delivery of new features, bug fixes and improvements. It operationalizes agile: the product is kept in a deployable state at all times and is improved continually with minimal manual intervention. The aim is to build, deploy and maintain the product with as little friction as possible, so agility reaches operations as well as development.

head: Practice
What it means
What it gives
rows: Development, testing and operations teams collaborate closely instead of working in silos
Software developed, deployed and monitored efficiently and reliably; a seamless, automated release
New features or fixes released to production in small, incremental changes
Fast feedback from real users; agility in development and operations
Performance metrics, user behaviour and system health tracked constantly
Feedback that lets the team improve the product iteratively

rows.label: Feedback
values: Fast, from real users and production data

teach.h: A small change, end to end
teach.caption: Each small release produces real-user feedback that feeds the next iteration.

teach.body: Continuous delivery grew up in software, where automated builds and tests make small releases cheap. PRINCE2 Agile warns that testing approaches must be transferred carefully to other products: a process change, a training course or a campaign cannot be rebuilt in minutes. The idea still applies, frequent small changes with fast feedback, but the mechanics are adapted to the product.

teach.h: Worked scenario: Pinewick Home and Garden's click and collect
teach.body: The e-commerce team releases small changes several times a week; Kieran Walsh, responsible for website stability, wants a weekly change board. A DevOps answer brings Kieran's operations staff into sprint reviews and release design, automates tests and checks so each release is seamless, and adds production monitoring of performance, customer behaviour and system health. Stability and speed are then managed together, and real customer data steers the next sprint rather than internal opinion.

teach.text: Traps: DevOps is shared responsibility, not handing all control to developers or to operations. Continuous delivery means small, frequent releases with fast real-user feedback, not saving everything for one big release. Monitoring data goes back to the development team. Feedback should come from real users, not internal opinions alone.

items: Goal: rapid, automated delivery; product always deployable; minimal manual effort.
DevOps: development, testing and operations collaborate; release is seamless and automated.
Continuous delivery: small incremental releases to production; fast feedback from real users.
Production monitoring (performance, behaviour, health) feeds development.
Transfer the ideas carefully to non-software products.

summary: You can now apply continuous agile development and operations to a scenario: DevOps collaboration, small automated releases with fast user feedback, and production monitoring that feeds the next iteration. You can also spot options that create silos or delay feedback.

A.q: Pinewick Home and Garden's e-commerce team deploys small website changes several times a week. Kieran Walsh, the IT operations manager, wants every change held for a weekly change board because of past outages. Which action BEST applies continuous agile development and operations?
options: Batch all changes into one quarterly release
Let the e-commerce team run operations itself
Share automated releases with operations
Give IT operations full control of all releases
A.why: DevOps has development, testing and operations teams collaborate closely so software is developed, deployed and monitored reliably, with a seamless, automated release process (14.2.2.2).

whyNot.0: A quarterly batch replaces small incremental releases and delays feedback from real users.
whyNot.1: Cutting operations out keeps a silo; DevOps is shared work between the teams.
whyNot.3: Handing one team full control is still a silo, not close collaboration.

A.q: Draycott Precision Engineering's software team releases small improvements to the live dashboard every week after Release 1. What is the main benefit of releasing in this way?
options: Fewer tests are needed for each change
Fast feedback from engineers' real use
The board approves each change in advance
Release planning workshops are not needed
A.why: Continuous delivery releases new features or fixes to production in small, incremental changes so the team gets fast feedback from real users (14.2.2.2).

whyNot.0: Small releases are still tested; the practice relies on automation, not fewer checks.
whyNot.2: Advance board approval of every change is not a feature of continuous delivery.
whyNot.3: Release planning at stage boundaries still has a purpose; this is about feedback.

A.q: Larkspur Rail's data team watches the matching model in production, tracking response times, how passengers use the claim screen and system health. What should happen to this information?
options: It goes to the board at the next stage boundary
It is kept by IT operations for audit purposes
It is included in the end project report
It feeds the team's next improvements
A.why: Continuous development is closely linked to monitoring in production: performance metrics, user behaviour and system health feed back to the development team to improve the product iteratively (14.2.2.2).

whyNot.0: Waiting for a stage boundary slows the feedback loop the monitoring exists for.
whyNot.1: Keeping the data within operations recreates a silo; it must reach development.
whyNot.2: The end project report reviews project performance; production data is for continual improvement.

B.q: Callowmere University's Northmere integration team builds the records link separately, and the university's IT operations staff see the code for the first time on go-live day. Which feature of continuous agile development and operations is missing?
options: Close collaboration of development, testing and operations
A fixed-price contract with the supplier for each iteration
A detailed release plan approved by the project board
A separate operations project after the hub goes live
B.why: With DevOps, development, testing and operations teams collaborate closely rather than working in silos, so software is developed, deployed and monitored reliably (14.2.2.2).

whyNot.1: The commercial model does not fix the silo between developers and operations.
whyNot.2: Board approval of a release plan does not create day-to-day collaboration.
whyNot.3: A later operations project extends the silo instead of removing it.

B.q: Easterholm County Council's digital team wants to adopt continuous agile development and operations for Care Online after Release 1. Which statement BEST describes the aim?
options: Release less often so each release is fully checked
Freeze the service once the final release is live
Involve as many staff as possible in every release
Keep it deployable with little manual effort
B.why: The practices aim at rapid, automated delivery, keeping the product always in a deployable state and continually improved with minimal manual intervention (14.2.2.2).

whyNot.0: Releasing less often works against rapid, incremental delivery.
whyNot.1: The product is continually improved after release, not frozen.
whyNot.2: Collaboration should be close and efficient, not as large as possible.

B.q: Draycott Precision Engineering's software team proposes to finish every dashboard feature for Factory B and release them all together at month 12. Which statement BEST explains why this conflicts with continuous agile development and operations?
options: Releases should be approved by the quality director
Factory B should wait for a separate project
Small, frequent releases give fast user feedback
Large releases need a formal change variation
B.why: Continuous delivery releases features in small, incremental changes to get fast feedback from real users (14.2.2.2).

whyNot.0: Independent quality checks matter, but they are not the reason a single big release conflicts with continuous delivery.
whyNot.1: Factory B is in this project's scope; the problem is the release pattern.
whyNot.3: No PRINCE2 Agile rule ties release size to contract variations.

C.q: Pinewick Home and Garden's IT operations manager proposes that the e-commerce team stops releasing changes itself and sends everything to his weekly change board, with no operations staff at sprint reviews. Is this an appropriate application of continuous agile development and operations, and why?
options: Yes, because IT operations is responsible for website stability
Yes, because a weekly batch gives customers faster feedback
No, because the change board belongs to the project board
No, because development and operations should work together
C.why: DevOps has development, testing and operations collaborate closely so release is seamless and automated; this proposal keeps them apart and slows feedback (14.2.2.2).

whyNot.0: Kieran is responsible for stability, but that is a reason to collaborate, not to separate the teams.
whyNot.1: Holding changes for a weekly batch slows feedback from real users.
whyNot.2: The verdict is right but the reason is wrong: the change board is not a project board body.

C.q: Draycott Precision Engineering's software team invites maintenance engineers and IT operations staff to every sprint review and automates the deployment of dashboard updates. Is this an appropriate application of continuous agile development and operations, and why?
options: Yes, because it joins development and operations
Yes, because engineers then sign off each change
No, because operations should join after closure
No, because automation removes the need for tests
C.why: DevOps brings development, testing and operations together so software is developed, deployed and monitored reliably, with an automated release process (14.2.2.2).

whyNot.1: Written sign-off of every change is not the reason this is good practice.
whyNot.2: Operations should collaborate throughout, not wait for the project to end.
whyNot.3: Automation supports testing; it does not remove it, and this is not a reason to reject the approach.

C.q: After Larkspur Rail's Release 2, the app team decides to judge the automatic payment feature by asking a few internal managers for their views, rather than looking at production data and passenger use. Is this an appropriate application of continuous agile development and operations, and why?
options: Yes, because managers understand the contract targets
Yes, because the passenger panel tested early versions
No, because real users and live data should guide it
No, because feedback is collected at the closure workshop
C.why: Continuous delivery seeks fast feedback from real users, and production monitoring of performance, behaviour and health feeds the team (14.2.2.2).

whyNot.0: Managers do know the targets, but internal opinion is not a substitute for real-user feedback.
whyNot.1: Earlier panel testing was useful, but it does not show how the live feature performs.
whyNot.3: The verdict is right but the reason is wrong: feedback is continuous, not saved for closure.

reteach.title: A food truck that tweaks its menu daily
reteach.question: How does a busy food truck keep improving without ever closing for a big relaunch?

blocks.body: The cook and the person at the hatch plan together each morning. A new sauce is tried on today's menu, not saved for a grand relaunch. Sales, queue times and what people leave on their plates are watched all day, and tomorrow's menu changes. The truck is always ready to serve: that is the spirit of continuous development and operations.

blocks.text: Asking the owner's friends what they think is not the same as watching what real customers buy. Feedback should come from real users.

explain.body: Continuous agile development and operations enables rapid, automated delivery of features, fixes and improvements, keeping the product always deployable and improving it with minimal manual intervention.

test.q: Saltmarsh Housing Group's digital team wants the tenant portal to be releasable at any moment, with routine releases needing very little manual work. Which concept does this describe?
options: Agile product management with a roadmap
Continuous agile development and operations
Transition from the project to operations
Managing product delivery with work packages
test.why: Continuous agile development and operations keeps a product always deployable and continually improved with minimal manual intervention (14.2.2.2).

whyNot.0: Agile product management steers the roadmap and priorities, not the release mechanics.
whyNot.2: Transition to operations is the hand-over of products, artifacts and procedures at the end of delivery.
whyNot.3: Managing product delivery is the PRINCE2 process linking the PM and a delivery team.

explain.body: Instead of working in silos, development, testing and operations teams collaborate closely so software is developed, deployed and monitored efficiently and reliably. The release process becomes seamless and automated.

test.q: Larkspur Rail's app team and the IT operations team agree to plan releases together, share automated tests and jointly watch the app in production. Which practice are they applying?
options: Continuous delivery
Swarming
DevOps
Refactoring
test.why: DevOps is close collaboration between development, testing and operations, with a seamless, automated release process (14.2.2.2).

whyNot.0: Continuous delivery is about small, frequent releases to production; the joint working described is DevOps.
whyNot.1: Swarming is a team focusing together on a blocker, not development and operations working together.
whyNot.3: Refactoring improves internal structure without changing behaviour.

explain.body: New features or fixes are released to production in small, incremental changes, giving the team fast feedback from real users and agility in both development and operations.

test.q: Callowmere University's web team releases each small improvement to the live hub as soon as it is done and tested, rather than bundling them. What does this practice MAINLY provide?
options: Fast feedback from real students
Fewer releases for operations to manage
A fixed release calendar for the board
Lower testing effort per change
test.why: Continuous delivery releases small, incremental changes so the team gets fast feedback from real users (14.2.2.2).

whyNot.1: It produces more frequent releases, not fewer.
whyNot.2: Releases follow readiness, not a fixed calendar set by the board.
whyNot.3: Each change is still tested; the gain is fast feedback.

explain.body: Performance metrics, user behaviour data and system health are tracked constantly in production and fed back to the development team so it can improve the product iteratively.

test.q: Draycott Precision Engineering's live dashboard shows that engineers rarely open the alert history page and that one gateway often drops its connection. Under continuous agile development and operations, what should happen NEXT with this data?
options: File it until the next annual review
Feed it back to the development team
Report it to the closed project board
Pass it to the union for comment
test.why: Production data on user behaviour and system health is fed back to the development team to improve the product iteratively (14.2.2.2).

whyNot.0: Filing it for an annual review delays the feedback loop.
whyNot.2: The project board no longer governs the live product.
whyNot.3: Engagement with staff representatives matters, but the data's purpose here is to steer the next improvement.
